stage_description: The end-of-life stage arrives when chronic or incurable disease (end-stage kidney disease, cancer, severe arthritis) limits quality of life. Care centers on palliative support: pain relief, comfort, and appetite. Cats tend to hide pain, so an honest quality-of-life assessment with the veterinarian and a timely, humane decision are essential.
nutrition: Feed to appetite: warm, aromatic food, a quiet calm feeding spot, and vet-prescribed appetizing or therapeutic diets if needed. The priority is enjoyment of food and adequate hydration rather than strict dietary targets.
activity: Calm, warmth, and easy access to water, litter, and hiding spots without needing to jump. Gentle contact as the cat wishes; the goal of this stage is comfort and companionship, not activity.
veterinary_check_frequency: Frequent veterinary contact to manage pain and symptoms on an individualized palliative-care plan, sometimes weekly or more often. A hospice plan and objective quality-of-life criteria are discussed.
dental_care: Gentle mouth care for comfort; painful dental procedures are deferred unless they improve well-being. Offer soft or moist food if the mouth is sore.
warning_signs: Refusing food and water, uncontrolled pain, labored breathing, stopping self-grooming, hiding, and complete apathy. These signs call for an urgent quality-of-life discussion with the veterinarian.
disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and does not replace consultation with a veterinarian.
